title: Three Paths, Three Kinds of People
hookLine: who is the path of action actually for? the Uddhava Gita answers: people who still want things
carry: karma yoga: the path for hearts that still want
tomorrow: a miser loses everything, and sings.

cards: Who is the path of action actually for? Deep in the dialogue, Uddhava asks something close to it. The Vedas, he says in effect, tell people what to do and what not to do.
They praise good works, and they also speak of a state beyond works altogether. So which is it? Do something, or stop doing?
It sounds like a question that needs a side. Krishna doesn't pick one. He looks at the people asking, and sorts the paths by who's walking them.

teach.b: Krishna says he has given three yogas, three paths, so people can reach the good: jnana, the path of knowing; karma, the path of action; and bhakti, the path of devotion. Then the sorting.
Jnana suits those who have grown weary of action and turned away from it.

teach.h: ACTION IS FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.
teach.b: Karma suits those who haven't, whose hearts still hold desires, who still want things from the world.
And bhakti suits someone who, by some good fortune, has come to love hearing about him, neither fed up with the world nor tied too tightly to it. Sit with that middle line.
The path of action isn't reserved for finished saints. It's for people with ambitions, a to-do list, a pull toward the world. The Uddhava Gita doesn't scold that wanting.
It gives it a road. How long does a person stay on it?

teach.h: STAY UNTIL WEARY, OR UNTIL FAITH WAKES.
teach.b: The very next verse answers: keep doing the work until you grow weary of it, or until faith in hearing his stories wakes up. Two ways off the road, and no deadline.
For someone in the middle of a busy life, it's a quietly kind teaching. It doesn't say drop everything first, then you can begin.
It says begin where your wanting already is.

how: Hindu teachers speak of three paths, jnana, karma and bhakti, and some say a student's temperament and stage of life help decide which path to emphasize, drawing on teachings like this one in the Bhagavata's eleventh book.

o: a path only for monks who own nothing
the path of action, for hearts that still want
the path of study for weary scholars

games.q: three paths, three kinds of people — tap the pairs.
p: for hearts that still want things
for those who love hearing of him
how long to walk the road of action
until weariness, or until faith wakes

s: in the Uddhava Gita, the path of action is for people who've stopped wanting things
it's for those whose hearts still hold desires and who aren't weary of action.
Krishna matches each of the three paths to a kind of person
knowing for the weary, action for those still wanting, devotion for those who love hearing of him.
Krishna says to drop all work before beginning
he says to keep working until weariness comes or faith wakes up.

games.q: you're busy, ambitious and not tired of the world at all. which of the three paths does the Uddhava Gita say suits you?
o: none yet; come back when you're weary.
games.why: karma: Krishna gives the path of action to people whose hearts still want things, and tells them to stay on it until weariness or faith arrives.

practice: Without judging it, let one thing you want rise up, a result at work, a change at home, something you're building, and look at it clearly, the way you'd look at a road from the top of a hill.
Then ask what one honest piece of work this wanting is asking of you. If you pray, you can offer that wanting, just as it is, to the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Karma. In the Uddhava Gita, the path of action: for hearts that still want things, walked until weariness comes or faith wakes up.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the path, or discipline, of action; one of the three yogas Krishna names to Uddhava.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga, the path for hearts that still want. Begin where your wanting is. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.20.1–5 (Uddhava asks how the Veda's commands to act fit with its praise of what lies beyond action)
Bhagavata Purana 11.20.6–8 (three yogas: jnana for the weary of action, karma for those with desires, bhakti for those who by fortune love hearing of him)
Bhagavata Purana 11.20.9 (perform action until weariness arises or faith in hearing his stories awakens)
